summary.text: The disproof iterates odd cyclic matrices of the form \(I+\tfrac12P\) to build full-rank dyadic lattices with controlled short integer relations, column sum \((3/2)^h\), and determinant \((1+2^{-(2m+1)})^{1+(2m+1)+\cdots+(2m+1)^{h-1}}\), which can be made arbitrarily small relative to the column sum. Balancing and perturbing these lattices yields digit-injective coefficient vectors, whose binary expansions give sum-distinct sets satisfying \(2^{|A|}/N>k\) for every \(k\), so no uniform constant can exist.

full_proof.text:
We disprove the asserted uniform lower bound by constructing, for every integer multiplier \(k\ge 0\), a positive integer \(N\) and a sum-distinct set \(A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}\) such that
\[
        kN<2^{|A|}.
\]
This makes the ratio \(2^{|A|}/N\) arbitrarily large, which is exactly the negation of the claimed estimate.

The construction proceeds through a family of lattices. All matrices below act on column vectors.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. An odd cyclic rigidity lemma
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Fix \(m\ge 0\), and put
\[
        d=2m+1.
\]
Coordinates indexed by \(0,1,\ldots,2m\) are understood cyclically, so the predecessor of \(0\) is \(2m\). Define the \(d\times d\) real matrix \(P_m\) by
\[
 (P_m u)_0=u_0+\frac12u_{2m},\qquad
 (P_m u)_i=u_i+\frac12u_{i-1}\quad(1\le i\le 2m).
\]
Thus \(2P_m u\) has coordinates \(2u_i+u_{i-1}\), cyclically.

We need two properties of this map.

First, \(P_m\) is admissible in the following sense:
\[
 z\in\mathbb Z^d,\quad |(P_mz)_i|<1\ \text{for every }i
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad z=0.                         \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, suppose more generally that integers \(z_i\) satisfy
\[
        |2z_i+z_{i-1}|<2                              \tag{2}
\]
for every cyclic index \(i\). If \(z_i\ne0\), then (2) forces \(z_{i-1}\ne0\) and forces \(z_{i-1}\) to have the opposite sign from \(z_i\). To see this, if \(z_i\ge1\) and \(z_{i-1}\ge0\), then \(2z_i+z_{i-1}\ge2\), contrary to (2); if \(z_i\le-1\) and \(z_{i-1}\le0\), the same argument with signs reversed applies. Moreover, the predecessor cannot be zero, since then \(|2z_i|\ge2\).

Consequently, starting from any nonzero coordinate and moving around the cycle, every coordinate is nonzero and the signs alternate at every step. After traversing a cycle of odd length, one returns to the starting coordinate with the opposite sign, an impossibility. Hence every \(z_i\) is zero. This proves (1).

We also require a strengthened “strip” form of this fact.

**Strip lemma.** Suppose \(u_0\in\mathbb R\), while \(u_1,\ldots,u_{2m}\in\mathbb Z\), and suppose
\[
        |2u_i+u_{i-1}|<2                              \tag{3}
\]
for every cyclic index \(i\). Then
\[
        \left|\sum_{i=0}^{2m}u_i\right|<1.            \tag{4}
\]

Here is a proof. First choose an index \(j\) at which \(|u_j|\) is maximal. From
\[
 2u_j=(2u_j+u_{j-1})-u_{j-1}
\]
and (3), we get
\[
 2|u_j|<2+|u_{j-1}|\le 2+|u_j|,
\]
so \(|u_j|<2\). Thus every \(|u_i|<2\). In particular,
\[
        u_i\in\{-1,0,1\}\qquad(1\le i\le2m).         \tag{5}
\]

We next show \(|u_0|<1\). Assume first that \(u_0\ge1\), and suppose \(m>0\). The inequality at coordinate \(0\), together with (5), forces \(u_{2m}=-1\). Replace \(u_0\) by the integer \(1\), leaving all other coordinates unchanged. Call the resulting integer vector \(w\). At coordinate \(0\), its cyclic expression is \(2-1=1\), of absolute value less than \(2\). At coordinate \(1\), (3), \(u_0\ge1\), and \(u_1\in\{-1,0,1\}\) imply that \(u_1\) is either \(-1\) or \(0\), and therefore \(|2u_1+1|<2\). At every later coordinate, the cyclic expression for \(w\) is unchanged from that for \(u\). Thus \(w\) is an integral vector satisfying (2), while \(w_0=1\), contradicting the odd-cycle rigidity. Hence \(u_0<1\). Applying the same argument to \(-u\) gives \(u_0>-1\). The case \(m=0\) follows immediately from \(|3u_0|<2\). Thus in all cases \(|u_0|<1\).

For successive integral tail coordinates, (3) and (5) imply
\[
        u_{i+1}=0\quad\text{or}\quad u_{i+1}=-u_i
                                                        \tag{6}
\]
whenever both coordinates lie in the tail. An elementary induction using (6) shows that the sum of the tail is either \(0\) or its first term:
\[
        \sum_{i=1}^{2m}u_i\in\{0,u_1\}.               \tag{7}
\]
Indeed, adjoining a new term either leaves the current alternating block unchanged by adding zero, or cancels its predecessor; induction gives precisely the two possibilities in (7).

If the tail sum is zero, (4) follows from \(|u_0|<1\). If it equals \(u_1\), then \(u_1\in\{-1,0,1\}\), and the inequality
\[
        |2u_1+u_0|<2
\]
can be checked in these three cases to give \(|u_0+u_1|<1\). This proves the strip lemma.

The matrix \(P_m\) has three further elementary properties. Every column sum is
\[
        \frac32.                                      \tag{8}
\]
Its entries are half-integers. Finally,
\[
        \det P_m=1+2^{-d}.                             \tag{9}
\]
For (9), write \(P_m=I+\frac12Q\), where \(Q\) is the permutation matrix of a single \(d\)-cycle (up to transpose, which does not alter the determinant). In the determinant expansion, a proper nonempty selection of cycle edges cannot form a permutation: once one cycle edge is chosen, bijectivity forces all of them to be chosen. Thus only the identity term and the full-cycle term survive. A \(d\)-cycle has sign \((-1)^{d-1}=1\), because \(d\) is odd. Hence the determinant is \(1+2^{-d}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Iterating the cyclic block
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Call a square real matrix \(C\) **admissible** if
\[
 z\in\mathbb Z^s,
 \quad |(Cz)_i|<1\text{ for all }i
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad z=0.                      \tag{10}
\]
We now define a lifting operation that replaces an admissible \(s\times s\) matrix by an admissible \(ds\times ds\) matrix.

For each old index \(i\), introduce one anchor variable \(x_i\) and \(2m\) tail variables \(x_{i,j}\), \(1\le j\le2m\). Put
\[
        t_i=x_i+\sum_{j=1}^{2m}x_{i,j}.                \tag{11}
\]
A change-of-variables map sends \(x\) to \(y\), where
\[
 y_{i,j}=x_{i,j},
 \qquad
 y_{i,0}=(Ct)_i-\sum_{j=1}^{2m}x_{i,j}.                \tag{12}
\]
In block form this change matrix is
\[
 \begin{pmatrix} C&U\\0&I\end{pmatrix},

a block upper-triangular matrix whose determinant is \(\det C\). Next, separately for every old index \(i\), apply \(P_m\) to the block
\[
        (y_{i,0},y_{i,1},\ldots,y_{i,2m}).
\]
The resulting matrix is denoted \(L_m(C)\).

We verify admissibility. Suppose \(x\) is integral and every coordinate of \(L_m(C)x\) has absolute value less than \(1\). For each \(i\), the tail coordinates \(y_{i,j}=x_{i,j}\) are integers, while the anchor \(y_{i,0}\) need only be regarded as real. The strip lemma therefore gives
\[
 \left|\sum_{j=0}^{2m}y_{i,j}\right|<1.

By (12), this sum is exactly \((Ct)_i\). Hence \(|(Ct)_i|<1\) for every \(i\). Since \(C\) is admissible, \(t=0\). Equations (11) and (12) then give \(y=x\). For each block, we now have \(|P_m x_i|<1\) and an integral input vector, so (1) gives that the entire block is zero. Thus \(x=0\), proving that \(L_m(C)\) is admissible.

The other data of the lift follow directly from its block form:
\[
 \det L_m(C)=(\det P_m)^s\det C,                       \tag{13}
\]
if every column of \(C\) has sum \(q\), then every column of \(L_m(C)\) has sum
\[
        \frac32q,                                      \tag{14}
\]
and if \(2^rC\) is integral, then \(2^{r+1}L_m(C)\) is integral. For (14), the change matrix preserves the common column sum \(q\), and the block-diagonal application of \(P_m\) multiplies all column sums by \(3/2\).

Start with the \(1\times1\) identity matrix and iterate this lift \(h\) times. Denote the resulting matrix by \(C_{m,h}\). Induction using the preceding facts gives:

* its dimension is
\[
        s=d^h=(2m+1)^h;                                \tag{15}
\]
* it is admissible;
* every column sum is
\[
        q_h=(3/2)^h;                                   \tag{16}
\]
* \(2^h C_{m,h}\) is an integral matrix;
* and
\[
 \det C_{m,h}
  =\left(1+2^{-d}\right)^{1+d+\cdots+d^{h-1}}.         \tag{17}
\]

For each fixed \(h\), this determinant tends to \(1\) as \(m\to\infty\). Indeed, with
\[
 E_{m,h}=1+d+\cdots+d^{h-1},

the inequality \(1+x\le e^x\) gives
\[
 \det C_{m,h}\le \exp(E_{m,h}2^{-d}).                  \tag{18}
\]
For fixed \(h\), \(E_{m,h}\) grows only polynomially in \(d=2m+1\), whereas \(2^{-d}\) decays exponentially, so the exponent in (18) tends to zero.

Consequently, for every given \(k\), we may first choose \(h>0\) so large that
\[
        (3/2)^h>2k,

after which we choose \(m>0\) so large that
\[
        \det C_{m,h}<2.

Then
\[
        k\det C_{m,h}<(3/2)^h=q_h.                    \tag{19}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. From the real matrix to a small-determinant integral lattice
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We record a general conversion. Let \(C\) be an admissible \((n+1)\times(n+1)\) real matrix such that:

1. every column sum is the same positive number \(q\);
2. \(\det C>0\);
3. \(R C\) is integral, where \(R=2^r\);
4. \(k\det C<q\).

Set
\[
        G=RC\in M_{n+1}(\mathbb Z).
\]
Every column of \(G\) has real, and hence integral, sum \(Rq\). Define an \(n\times n\) integer matrix
\[
        B_{ij}=G_{i+1,j+1}-G_{i+1,0}
        \qquad(0\le i,j<n).                            \tag{20}
\]

A standard determinant reduction gives
\[
        \det G=(Rq)\det B.                             \tag{21}
\]
For completeness, replace the first row of \(G\) by the sum of all its rows; this leaves the determinant unchanged and makes that row constant, equal to \(Rq\). Then subtract column \(0\) from every other column. The first row becomes \((Rq,0,\ldots,0)\), and the remaining minor is precisely \(B\). Expanding along the first row proves (21).

On the other hand, \(\det G=R^{n+1}\det C\). Cancelling \(R>0\) in (21) gives
\[
        q\det B=R^n\det C.                             \tag{22}
\]
Therefore \(\det B>0\), and from \(k\det C<q\) we obtain
\[
        k\det B<R^n=2^{nr}.                            \tag{23}
\]

The matrix \(B\) also has the following balanced admissibility property:
\[
 \left.
 \begin{array}{l}
 |(Bz)_i|<R\quad(0\le i<n),\\[2mm]
 \left|\sum_i(Bz)_i\right|<R
 \end{array}
 \right\}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad z=0.                      \tag{24}
\]
To prove this, define
\[
        w=\left(-\sum_jz_j,z_0,\ldots,z_{n-1}\right).
\nFor rows \(1,\ldots,n\), formula (20) gives
\[
        (Gw)_{i+1}=(Bz)_i.                             \tag{25}
\]
Because every column of \(G\) has the same sum and the coordinates of \(w\) sum to zero, the coordinates of \(Gw\) sum to zero. Thus
\[
        (Gw)_0=-\sum_i(Bz)_i.                          \tag{26}
\]
The hypotheses in (24) therefore say that every coordinate of \(Gw\) has absolute value less than \(R\). Since \(G=RC\), division by \(R\) shows that every coordinate of \(Cw\) has absolute value less than \(1\). Admissibility of \(C\) gives \(w=0\), and hence \(z=0\).

We may put \(B\) into triangular form using unimodular column operations without losing (24). Here are the relevant details. Given a nonsingular integer matrix, choose, among all nonzero entries obtainable in the first row by unimodular column operations, one of smallest positive absolute value and move it to the first position. If it did not divide some other first-row entry, the Euclidean remainder could be produced by a column shear followed by a swap, yielding a smaller nonzero first entry. Hence this pivot divides every other entry in the first row. Integer column shears can then clear the remainder of that row. Applying the same argument inductively to the lower-right minor gives a unimodular matrix \(U\) such that \(BU\) is lower triangular. Reversing the orders of both rows and columns makes it upper triangular. Multiplication on the right by a diagonal matrix with one diagonal entry \(-1\), if necessary, orients its determinant.

Unimodular right multiplication preserves (24): if \(T=BU\) and \(Tz\) obeys the two bounds, then \(B(Uz)\) obeys them, so \(Uz=0\); unimodularity then gives \(z=0\). Simultaneously reversing rows and columns merely reindexes coordinates and also preserves the sum of the coordinates. Thus we obtain an upper-triangular integer matrix \(T\) such that
\[
 (-1)^n\det T=D>0,
 \qquad D=\det B,                                     \tag{27}
\]
which still satisfies balanced admissibility with radius \(R\), and by (23),
\[
        kD<2^{nr}.                                     \tag{28}
\]
The factor \((-1)^n\) in (27) is a convenient orientation for a later cofactor computation.

Define, for \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\), the \((n+1)\)-vector
\[
 L_T(z)=\bigl((Tz)_0,\ldots,(Tz)_{n-1},
              -\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(Tz)_i\bigr).          \tag{29}
\]
Balanced admissibility says exactly that if every coordinate of \(L_T(z)\) has absolute value less than \(R\), then \(z=0\). Equivalently,
\[
 z\ne0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \max_i |L_T(z)_i|\ge R=2^r.                          \tag{30}
\]

Applying this entire conversion to \(C=C_{m,h}\), with \(r=h\), \(q=(3/2)^h\), and using (19), produces, for every \(k\), integers \(n,r,D\) and an upper-triangular integer matrix \(T\) satisfying (27), (28), and (30).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. A primitive hyperplane and bounded positive coefficients
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Fix such a matrix \(T\). We now turn its lattice gap into digit weights.

Define the integral automorphism \(\beta:\mathbb Z^{n+1}\to\mathbb Z^{n+1}\) by
\[
 \beta(x_0,\ldots,x_n)
 =\left(x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1},x_n-\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}x_i\right).     \tag{31}
\]
Its inverse adds the sum of the first \(n\) coordinates to the last coordinate.

Let \(S\) be the \((n+1)\times(n+1)\) matrix obtained by placing \(T\) in rows \(0,\ldots,n-1\) and columns \(1,\ldots,n\), with all other entries zero. Since \(T\) is upper triangular, \(S\) is strictly upper triangular. Therefore, for every integer \(t\),
\[
        U_t=I+tS                                      \tag{32}
\]
is upper triangular with all diagonal entries \(1\), and hence
\[
        \det U_t=1.                                   \tag{33}
\]
In particular, \(U_t\) is an integral automorphism.

For \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\), put
\[
        \Phi_t(z)=\beta\bigl(U_t(0,z)\bigr).           \tag{34}
\]
Directly from the definitions,
\[
        \Phi_t(z)=tL_T(z)+\beta(0,z).                  \tag{35}
\]

We need to control the error term. Let
\[
 A_T=\sum_{i,j}|\operatorname{adj}(T)_{ij}|,
 \qquad E=(n+1)A_T.                                   \tag{36}
\]
If
\[
        M=\max_i|L_T(z)_i|,

the first \(n\) coordinates in (29) show that \(|(Tz)_i|\le M\). Since
\[
        (\det T)z=\operatorname{adj}(T)Tz

a coordinatewise estimate, together with \(|\det T|\ge1\), gives
\[
        |z_j|\le A_T M.                               \tag{37}
\]
The first \(n\) coordinates of \(\beta(0,z)\) are among \(0,z_0,\ldots,z_{n-2}\), depending only on the chosen ordering, and its final coordinate is one coordinate minus the sum of the preceding ones. The triangle inequality and (37) therefore give the uniform estimate
\[
        |\beta(0,z)_i|\le EM\quad\text{for every }i.  \tag{38}
\]

If \(z\ne0\), choose a coordinate at which \(|L_T(z)_i|=M\). By (30), \(M\ge R\). From (35) and (38), for every \(t\ge E\),
\[
 \max_i|\Phi_t(z)_i|
 \ge tM-EM
 =(t-E)M
 \ge(t-E)R.                                          \tag{39}
\]
Thus, whenever
\[
        q\le(t-E)R,                                   \tag{40}
\]
there is no nonzero \(z\) for which all coordinates of \(\Phi_t(z)\) have absolute value less than \(q\).

The image \(\Phi_t(\mathbb Z^n)\) is a primitive rank-\(n\) sublattice of \(\mathbb Z^{n+1}\). An explicit primitive integral linear functional cutting it out is
\[
 \lambda_t(x)=\text{the first coordinate of }U_t^{-1}\beta^{-1}(x). \tag{41}
\]
Let
\[
        c_i(t)=\lambda_t(e_i),

the coefficients of this functional. Then
\[
        \lambda_t(x)=\sum_{i=0}^n c_i(t)x_i,           \tag{42}
\]
and
\[
 \lambda_t(x)=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 x=\Phi_t(z)\text{ for some }z\in\mathbb Z^n.         \tag{43}
\]
Indeed, \(\lambda_t(x)=0\) means that the first coordinate of \(U_t^{-1}\beta^{-1}x\) is zero, so that vector is uniquely of the form \((0,z)\); applying \(\beta U_t\) gives (43).

We next need positivity and an upper bound for the coefficients \(c_i(t)\). By Cramer's rule, because \(\det U_t=1\), \(c_i(t)\) is the determinant obtained from \(U_t\) by replacing its first column by \(\beta^{-1}(e_i)\). It is therefore a polynomial in \(t\) of degree at most \(n\). Its leading coefficient is independent of \(i\) and is
\[
        (-1)^n\,\det T=D.                             \tag{44}
\]
To see this explicitly, divide the determinant by \(t^n\). In the unreplaced columns, \(U_t/t=t^{-1}I+S\), so as \(t\to\infty\) these columns converge to those of \(S\). For every \(i\), the last coordinate of \(\beta^{-1}(e_i)\) is \(1\): if \(i<n\), the inverse operation adds the sum of the first \(n\) coordinates to the last, and if \(i=n\), the last coordinate was already \(1\). Expanding the limiting determinant along its final row leaves \(T\), with cofactor sign \((-1)^n\). This proves (44). Hence
\[
        \frac{c_i(t)}{t^n}\longrightarrow D
        \qquad(t\to+\infty)                           \tag{45}
\]
for every \(i\).

Now take
\[
        t=2^M+E                                       \tag{46}
\]
for a sufficiently large positive integer \(M\). Since there are only \(n+1\) coefficients, (45), equally with the harmless shift by \(E\), implies simultaneously that
\[
        0<c_i(t)\le 2D(2^M)^n
        \qquad(0\le i\le n).                          \tag{47}
\]
Set
\[
        a_i=c_i(t)\in\mathbb N,
        \qquad Q=2^{M+r}.                              \tag{48}
\]
Because \(t-E=2^M\) and \(R=2^r\), condition (40) holds with equality:
\[
        Q=(t-E)R.
\]

We claim that the weights \(a_0,\ldots,a_n\) distinguish all digit vectors with digits in \(\{0,\ldots,Q-1\}\):
\[
 \sum_i x_i a_i=\sum_i y_i a_i,
 \quad 0\le x_i,y_i<Q
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=y.                      \tag{49}
\]
Indeed, let \(v_i=x_i-y_i\). Then \(|v_i|<Q\), and (42) says \(\lambda_t(v)=0\). By (43), \(v=\Phi_t(z)\) for some \(z\). If \(z\ne0\), (39) says that some coordinate of \(v\) has absolute value at least \(Q\), a contradiction. Thus \(z=0\), so \(v=0\) and \(x=y\). This proves (49).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Binary expansion and the sum-distinct set
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Write
\[
        \ell=M+r.
\]
For each \(0\le i\le n\) and each \(0\le j<\ell\), form the positive integer
\[
        b_{i,j}=2^j a_i.                               \tag{50}
\]
Let \(A\) be the set of all these integers.

Every subset of the indexed family \(\{b_{i,j}\}\) determines, for each fixed \(i\), the binary digit
\[
        x_i=\sum_{j:\,b_{i,j}\text{ selected}}2^j,
        \qquad 0\le x_i<2^\ell=Q.                     \tag{51}
\]
The subset sum is then \(\sum_i x_i a_i\). If two indexed subsets have the same sum, (49) gives equality of all the digits \(x_i\), and uniqueness of binary expansion gives equality of the selected bits for every \((i,j)\). Thus all indexed subset sums are distinct. In particular the numbers \(b_{i,j}\) themselves are pairwise distinct: equality of two of them would equate the sums of two different singleton subsets. Therefore passing from the indexed family to the set \(A\) loses no elements, and
\[
        |A|=(n+1)(M+r).                                \tag{52}
\]
The same argument proves that all subset sums of the ordinary set \(A\) are distinct.

By (47) and \(j\le \ell-1\), every element of \(A\) is at most
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 N&=2^{M+r-1}\bigl(2D(2^M)^n\bigr)\\
  &=D\,2^{(n+1)M+r}.                                  \tag{53}
 \end{aligned}
\]
All elements are positive, so
\[
        A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}.
\]
Also \(N>0\).

Finally, using (28), (52), and (53),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 kN
   &=kD\,2^{(n+1)M+r}\\
   &<2^{nr}\,2^{(n+1)M+r}\\
   &=2^{(n+1)(M+r)}\\
   &=2^{|A|}.                                         \tag{54}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus for every natural number \(k\) we have constructed \(N>0\) and a sum-distinct set \(A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}\) for which \(kN<2^{|A|}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Contradiction to the proposed uniform constant
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Suppose, for contradiction, that there were a real constant \(C>0\) such that every nonempty-range sum-distinct pair \((A,N)\) satisfied
\[
        C2^{|A|}<N.                                   \tag{55}
\]
Choose a natural number \(k>C^{-1}\). The construction above gives \(A,N\) with
\[
        kN<2^{|A|}.
\nMultiplying (55) by \(C^{-1}>0\) gives
\[
        2^{|A|}<C^{-1}N<kN,

a contradiction.

Therefore no such positive constant \(C\) exists. Equivalently, the ratios \(2^{|A|}/N\) among finite sum-distinct subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\) are unbounded, which disproves the stated conjecture.
